title: Endocrine System
tagline: Major endocrine glands, their hormones, feedback control, and disorders such as diabetes and goitre.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class X Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: While the nervous system gives fast, short-lived control, the endocrine system gives slower but longer-lasting regulation through hormones secreted directly into the blood. This chapter covers the major glands and their hormones — pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal, pancreas and the gonads — together with the feedback principle that keeps hormone levels steady, and the disorders that follow from over- or under-secretion: goitre and cretinism from thyroid failure, diabetes from insulin deficiency, and the effects of adrenal cortical and medullary hormones.

facts.label: Master gland
facts.value: Pituitary — secretes tropic hormones controlling other glands

facts.label: Feedback
facts.value: High hormone level inhibits further release — negative feedback keeps levels steady

facts.label: Insulin
facts.value: Made by the pancreas (islets of Langerhans); low levels cause diabetes mellitus

learn.title: Major endocrine glands and their hormones

blocks.text: Endocrine glands are ductless and pour their secretion directly into the blood, which carries the hormone to its target organ. The pituitary at the base of the brain is the master gland: it secretes growth hormone, TSH and ACTH that control other endocrine glands, ADH controlling water reabsorption, and oxytocin. The thyroid in the neck secretes thyroxine, whose iodine-containing molecule raises the basal metabolic rate and, in children, is essential for normal growth and mental development; the parathyroids on its back surface secrete parathyroid hormone, which raises blood calcium by drawing it from bone. The adrenal glands above the kidneys have a cortex and a medulla: the cortex secretes adrenaline-related cortical hormones regulating salt and water balance and blood sugar, while the medulla secretes adrenaline, the 'fight or flight' hormone that raises heart rate, blood sugar and blood flow to muscles. The pancreas is both exocrine and endocrine: its islets of Langerhans secrete insulin, which lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake and glycogen storage, and glucagon, which raises it by breaking down glycogen. The gonads — testes and ovaries — secrete sex hormones responsible for secondary sexual characters and reproductive development at puberty.

items.meaning: Ductless gland secreting hormones directly into the blood.
Chemical messenger acting on a target organ at a distance.
Master gland controlling other endocrine glands via tropic hormones.
Thyroid hormone raising basal metabolic rate; needs iodine.
Medullary hormone preparing the body for emergency action.
Pancreatic hormone lowering blood glucose; deficiency causes diabetes mellitus.

items: Pituitary: growth hormone, TSH, ACTH, ADH, oxytocin — controls water balance, growth and other glands.
Thyroxine: raises metabolic rate; deficiency -> goitre (enlarged thyroid) and cretinism in children.
Parathyroid hormone: raises blood calcium by releasing it from bones.
Adrenal cortex: cortical hormones regulating salt/water balance and blood sugar.
Adrenal medulla: adrenaline — faster heart, higher blood sugar, dilated airways and muscle vessels.
Pancreas (islets of Langerhans): insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon raises it — antagonistic pair.
Gonads: testosterone (male) and oestrogen/progesterone (female) drive secondary sexual characters at puberty.

items.text: Startle or fright makes the heart pound and palms sweat within seconds — adrenaline release.
items.note: Faster than most hormone responses because the medulla is neurally triggered.

items.text: Goitre in regions with iodine-poor soil: without iodine no thyroxine is made, so TSH drives the thyroid to enlarge.
items.note: Iodised salt programmes exist precisely to prevent this.

blocks.text: Hormone levels are kept within narrow limits by negative feedback: when thyroxine in the blood rises above normal, the pituitary's TSH secretion is inhibited and the thyroid makes less; when thyroxine falls, TSH stimulates it again. The same principle governs insulin and blood glucose: rising glucose after a meal stimulates insulin release, which lowers glucose, which then reduces insulin secretion. Failure of these loops produces disease. Too little thyroxine in adults causes myxoedema (sluggishness, low metabolic rate); in children it causes cretinism — stunted growth and mental deficiency — preventable by early treatment; iodine deficiency causes goitre. Too little insulin, or cells that cannot respond to it, causes diabetes mellitus: blood glucose stays high, glucose is lost in urine, and the body oxidises fats instead, producing acidic ketones — hence the sweet urine, thirst and weight loss of untreated diabetes. Insulin injections treat insulin-dependent diabetes because the hormone is a protein that would be digested if swallowed.

items: Negative feedback: hormone level inhibits (or stimulates) its own controlling signal — stability.
Hypothyroidism: adults -> myxoedema; children -> cretinism (prevented by early thyroxine treatment).
Goitre: thyroid enlargement from iodine deficiency or TSH overstimulation.
Diabetes mellitus: insufficient insulin action -> high blood glucose, glucose in urine, ketone acidosis.
Diabetes symptoms: frequent urination, thirst, hunger, weight loss, slow healing.
Insulin is a protein — must be injected, not swallowed, or it is digested in the gut.
Hyperthyroidism (excess thyroxine): high metabolic rate, weight loss, irritability.

items.text: A diabetic on insulin must carry fast-acting sugar for hypoglycaemia — too much insulin drops blood glucose dangerously.
items.note: Both directions of the glucose curve are medically dangerous.

items.text: Adrenaline injections are given for severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis) because of rapid airway and heart effects.
items.note: The auto-injector delivers into the thigh muscle for fast absorption.

items.meaning: A rising level of a hormone inhibits the signals driving its release.
Thyroxine deficiency in childhood causing stunted growth and mental impairment.
Disorder of insulin action causing high blood glucose.

blocks.text: The two control systems complement each other. Nervous control is fast, precise and short-lived: impulses travel along neurons to specific effectors and act within milliseconds. Endocrine control is slower to start, travels via the blood to target organs chosen by chemical specificity, and its effects are widespread and long-lasting — minutes to hours or longer. Yet the systems interact at every level: the hypothalamus converts neural signals into releasing hormones that control the pituitary, so the brain steers the endocrine system; the adrenal medulla is triggered neurally by the sympathetic nervous system; and hormones such as adrenaline alter the sensitivity of neurons and organs. Coordination of growth, metabolism, reproduction and stress responses depends on both working together, with hormones providing sustained background regulation and nerves providing immediate precise response.

items: Nervous: electrical impulses, neurons, milliseconds, short-lived, precise targets.
Endocrine: chemical hormones, blood-borne, seconds to hours, widespread and sustained.
Hypothalamus is the neural-endocrine link: it controls pituitary hormone release.
Adrenal medulla is under direct sympathetic nervous control — neural trigger, hormonal broadcast.
Hormone specificity: only target cells with matching receptors respond.
Both systems maintain homeostasis — a stable internal environment despite external change.

items.text: Touching something hot: nervous withdrawal in milliseconds, then adrenal adrenaline sustains alertness.
items.note: Immediate neural response followed by slower hormonal reinforcement.

items.text: Growth depends on pituitary growth hormone but is steered by neural and nutritional signals — systems combined.
items.note: Deficiency of GH before puberty causes dwarfism; excess causes gigantism.

keyPoints: Endocrine glands are ductless; hormones travel in blood to target organs.
Pituitary is the master gland: growth hormone, TSH, ACTH, ADH, oxytocin.
Thyroxine raises metabolic rate; needs iodine; deficiency causes goitre and cretinism.
Adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline for 'fight or flight'; cortex regulates salts and sugar.
Pancreas: insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon raises it.
Negative feedback keeps hormone levels within narrow limits.
Diabetes mellitus = insufficient insulin action; insulin is injected because it is a protein.
Nervous control is fast and precise; endocrine control is slower, widespread and longer-lasting; the hypothalamus links them.
experimentFocus: Blood-sugar reasoning: meal -> glucose up -> insulin up -> glucose normal — trace any disturbance through the loop.
If insulin secretion stops, predict consequences: hyperglycaemia, glycosuria, ketone acidosis — each consequence separately earns marks.
Feedback questions: state the direction of change and which signal is inhibited or stimulated — 'negative feedback' without the mechanism earns little.
examFocus: Gland-hormone-effect triples must be memorised in both directions — questions name either the hormone or the effect.
Disorder answers: name the hormone imbalance, the symptom and the treatment (goitre-iodine, cretinism-early thyroxine, diabetes-insulin).
Why is insulin injected not swallowed? Because it is a protein digested in the stomach — a guaranteed mark if stated.
Compare nervous versus endocrine on speed, route, duration and specificity for full comparison marks.

Regulation where the product level controls its own production rate.

Childhood hypothyroidism causing growth and mental impairment.

questions.prompt: Which hormone regulates the basal metabolic rate?
questions.explanation: Thyroxine from the thyroid raises the basal metabolic rate and, in children, is essential for normal growth and brain development.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing adrenaline — it raises metabolic activity transiently in emergencies, but thyroxine sets the basal rate.

questions.prompt: Diabetes mellitus results from the deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Without enough insulin, or functioning response to it, blood glucose cannot be lowered — glucose stays high and appears in the urine.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing thyroxine — thyroid deficiency causes metabolic slowing, not high blood sugar.

questions.prompt: The 'fight or flight' hormone secreted by the adrenal medulla is:
questions.explanation: Adrenaline prepares the body for emergencies: faster heartbeat, raised blood sugar, dilated airways and increased blood to muscles.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing thyroxine — it changes metabolic rate gradually, not for emergencies.

options: Iodine deficiency leading to low thyroxine
questions.answer: Iodine deficiency leading to low thyroxine
questions.explanation: Without iodine the thyroid cannot synthesise thyroxine; the pituitary then over-secretes TSH and the gland enlarges — goitre.
questions.commonMistake: Saying 'overactive thyroid' — goitre is enlargement, most commonly from under-activity and iodine lack.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the ________ gland at the base of the brain is called the master gland because its hormones control other endocrine glands.
questions.explanation: The pituitary secretes TSH and ACTH that stimulate the thyroid and adrenal cortex respectively, alongside growth hormone, ADH and oxytocin.
questions.commonMistake: Saying hypothalamus — it controls the pituitary, but the 'master gland' title is the pituitary's.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: insulin is secreted by the ________ of the pancreas and acts to ________ blood glucose levels.
questions.explanation: The beta cells of the islets of Langerhans release insulin when blood glucose rises, promoting uptake and glycogen storage.
questions.commonMistake: Reversing the effect — insulin lowers glucose; glucagon raises it.

questions.prompt: Explain the principle of negative feedback using thyroxine as an example.
questions.answer: Negative feedback means that the level of a product controls the signals that produced it, keeping the level stable. For thyroxine: when the blood thyroxine concentration rises above normal, this is detected and the pituitary reduces its secretion of TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone); with less TSH acting on the thyroid gland, thyroxine production falls back toward normal. Conversely, when blood thyroxine falls too low, the inhibition is released and TSH secretion rises, stimulating the thyroid to produce more thyroxine. In this way any deviation from the set level triggers a response that counteracts it — a self-correcting loop that maintains homeostasis.
questions.explanation: The rising and falling halves must both be described — the loop works in both directions.
questions.commonMistake: Defining feedback without the corrective direction — examiners want the counteraction described explicitly.

questions.prompt: State two hormones of the pancreas, the effect of each on blood glucose, and explain why insulin must be injected rather than swallowed.
questions.answer: Insulin, secreted by the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans, LOWERS blood glucose by promoting the uptake of glucose by cells and its conversion to glycogen in the liver. Glucagon, secreted by the alpha cells, RAISES blood glucose by stimulating the breakdown of stored glycogen to glucose in the liver. Insulin must be injected because it is a protein hormone: if swallowed it would be digested by proteases in the stomach and small intestine into amino acids, losing its structure and therefore its ability to lower blood glucose. Injection delivers it directly into the blood where it remains intact and functional.
questions.explanation: The antagonistic pair plus the protein-digestion reason — the injection point is the highest-yield part of this question.
questions.commonMistake: Saying 'the stomach destroys it' without naming digestion of a protein — the molecule type is what earns the mark.

questions.prompt: Describe the disorders caused by thyroid under- and over-activity, and by insulin deficiency, naming the hormone involved in each.
questions.answer: Thyroxine (thyroid): deficiency in adults causes myxoedema — low basal metabolic rate, weight gain, sluggishness, cold intolerance and swelling of the face. Deficiency in young children causes cretinism — stunted physical growth and severe mental impairment — but this is preventable if treated early with thyroxine supplements. Iodine deficiency in the diet causes the thyroid to enlarge as the pituitary secretes excess TSH in an unsuccessful attempt to raise thyroxine — a goitre. Over-secretion of thyroxine causes hyperthyroidism: raised basal metabolic rate, rapid pulse, weight loss despite a good appetite, sweating and irritability. Insulin (pancreas): insufficient insulin secretion or cellular response causes diabetes mellitus, in which blood glucose remains high, glucose is lost in the urine causing frequent urination and thirst, and the body oxidises fats producing acidic ketones; untreated, this leads to ketoacidosis and weight loss, and is managed with insulin injections, dietary control and exercise.
questions.explanation: Each disorder paired with its hormone, its direction of imbalance and its treatment — organised answers collect every mark.
questions.commonMistake: Mixing up myxoedema (adult) and cretinism (child) — both are hypothyroidism but differ by age of onset.
